docs.title: Mastering Elite Engineering Workflows
docs.text: Last reviewed: 2026-11-24

docs.title: About this playbook
docs.text: This playbook helps engineering teams design and improve GitHub-centered workflows for code review, CI/CD, governance, repository structure, planning, measurement, and tool integration. Treat examples as starting points: adapt permissions, controls, release processes, and team expectations to your own environment before applying them.

docs.title: Who should use it
docs.text:
• Engineering leaders defining shared practices and governance.
  • Staff and principal engineers designing platforms, CI/CD, and repository architecture.
  • Senior engineers improving day-to-day delivery, code review, and developer experience.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository and review its contribution guidance and security policy.
  2. Install the documentation dependencies from the repository root and build the site: 
    python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs build --strict
  3. Choose the guide that matches the decision you are making. Use the implementation checklists as prompts, not universal compliance requirements.
  4. Copy only the relevant examples from examples/actions/ or templates/. The workflows in .github/workflows/ are for this repository’s documentation and security checks, not turnkey application pipelines.
  5. Before production use, verify action versions, permissions, secrets, required settings, and project-specific commands.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
• Code Review & Collaboration: risk-based review, reviewer responsibilities, response expectations, feedback, and adoption.
  • GitHub Actions & Automation: CI, deployment, reusable automation, security, and maintenance.
  • Governance & Security: access controls, repository policy, CODEOWNERS, and security operations.
  • Repository Structure: monorepo, polyrepo, dependency, visibility, and discovery decisions.
  • Metrics & Developer Experience: DORA, SPACE, surveys, data quality, and improvement loops.
  • Organizations & Project Planning: teams, permissions, GitHub Projects, and cross-repository work.
  • Complementary Tools & Integrations: tool selection, data ownership, integration security, and lifecycle.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text: Keep guidance concrete and reviewable. Separate required controls from optional examples. Do not copy a workflow without understanding its event triggers, permissions, secrets, runner trust, and deployment protections. Measure team systems to improve them; do not use raw activity metrics as individual quotas.

docs.title: Code Review & Collaboration: Elite Engineering Practices
Introduction
docs.text: Code review is a cornerstone of high-quality software development, serving as both a quality control mechanism and a knowledge-sharing practice. For elite engineering teams, code review is not merely a checkpoint but a collaborative process that enhances code quality, spreads knowledge, and builds team cohesion. This section outlines best practices for structuring code reviews, defining reviewer roles, optimizing review workflows, and integrating automation to create a scalable, efficient review process.

docs.title: Review Protocols by Change Type and Risk Level
Tiered Review Framework
docs.text:
Elite engineering teams implement a tiered review framework that scales the intensity of review based on the risk and complexity of changes:

  • Documentation (low risk): light review by one reviewer.
  • Test additions (low risk): standard review by one reviewer.
  • Bug fixes (medium risk): standard review by one or two reviewers.
  • New features (high risk): thorough review by at least two reviewers.
  • Core architecture (critical risk): deep review by at least two reviewers and an architect.
  • Security-related changes (critical risk): security review by at least two reviewers and a security specialist.

Use the separate response-time targets below as example starting points, not an additional risk-based SLA. Document local priority definitions, business hours, escalation, and exceptions in CONTRIBUTING.md. Enforce merge requirements with repository rules, not only with a template.

docs.title: Small Team Implementation (3-7 engineers)
docs.text: For small teams, simplify the framework to three tiers: - Light: Documentation, tests (1 reviewer) - Standard: Bug fixes, small features (1 reviewer) - Thorough: New features, architecture changes (all available team members)

docs.title: Scaling to Larger Teams (10-30+ engineers)
docs.text: As teams grow: - Introduce domain experts as required reviewers for specific areas - Implement CODEOWNERS to automatically assign reviewers - Add specialized review for cross-cutting concerns (performance, accessibility, security) - Consider a "review buddy" system for junior engineers

docs.title: Primary Reviewer
docs.text: The primary reviewer is responsible for: - Comprehensive code examination - Ensuring code meets functional requirements - Verifying test coverage - Checking for edge cases - Providing timely feedback (within SLA)

docs.title: Secondary Reviewer
docs.text: The secondary reviewer focuses on: - Architectural consistency - Design patterns - Performance implications - Security considerations - Cross-functional requirements

docs.title: Code Owner
docs.text: When using CODEOWNERS, the designated owner is automatically requested for review on matching pull requests, subject to GitHub's rules. A CODEOWNERS entry alone does not block merging. If owner approval is required, enable the corresponding required-code-owner-review rule in branch protection or a repository ruleset. Owners and teams also need the appropriate repository access. See GitHub's CODEOWNERS documentation.

docs.title: Expert Reviewer
docs.text: For specialized concerns: - Security expert: Reviews security-sensitive changes - Performance expert: Evaluates performance-critical code - Accessibility expert: Ensures accessibility standards - UX expert: Reviews user-facing changes

docs.title: Review response expectations
docs.text:
Set local expectations for acknowledging a review request and completing the review. There is no useful universal target based only on team size. Agree on working hours, priority labels, ownership and handoff, urgent-request escalation, and how the team will respond when review demand exceeds capacity. Measure first response separately from time to resolution, and revisit the agreement using actual workload and team feedback.

Implementation tip: Use labels or another visible signal for genuinely urgent changes. Keep an expedited path explicit and require a follow-up review rather than treating priority as permission to bypass controls.

docs.title: Reducing Review Bottlenecks
docs.text:
To maintain flow and prevent bottlenecks:

  1. Review rotation: Designate "review focus days" for team members
  2. Pair reviews: Conduct synchronous pair reviews for complex changes
  3. Time blocking: Schedule dedicated review time in calendars
  4. WIP limits: Limit the number of open PRs per developer
  5. Review swarms: For critical changes, gather the team for a focused review session

docs.title: Basic PR Template Structure
docs.text:
## Description
[Provide a brief description of the changes in this PR]

## Related Issues
[Link to any related issues, e.g., "Fixes #123"]

## Type of Change
- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation update

## How Has This Been Tested?
[Describe the tests that you ran]

## Checklist
- [ ] My code follows the project's style guidelines
- [ ] I have performed a self-review
- [ ] I have added tests that prove my fix/feature works
- [ ] New and existing tests pass locally
- [ ] Documentation has been updated (if applicable)

docs.title: Advanced PR Template for Larger Teams
docs.text:
For mid-sized to large teams, enhance the template with:

## Risk Assessment
- [ ] Low: Isolated change with minimal impact
- [ ] Medium: New feature with moderate scope
- [ ] High: Core functionality or wide-reaching changes

## Performance Considerations
[Describe any performance implications]

## Security Considerations
[Describe any security implications]

## Rollout Plan
- [ ] Standard deployment
- [ ] Phased rollout
- [ ] Feature flag controlled

## Post-Deployment Verification
[Describe how to verify the changes in production]

docs.title: Project-Specific Templates
docs.text:
Elite teams maintain specialized templates for different project types:

  • Frontend template: Includes browser compatibility, accessibility, and design fidelity checks
  • Backend template: Focuses on API contracts, database changes, and performance
  • Infrastructure template: Emphasizes security, scalability, and disaster recovery
  • Open-source template: Includes community impact, backward compatibility, and documentation

docs.title: Automated Checks
docs.text:
Integrate these automated checks into your PR workflow:

  1. Linting and formatting: Enforce code style consistency
  2. Unit and integration tests: Verify functionality
  3. Code coverage: Ensure adequate test coverage
  4. Static analysis: Identify potential bugs and vulnerabilities
  5. Dependency scanning: Check for vulnerable dependencies
  6. Performance benchmarks: Detect performance regressions

docs.title: GitHub Actions Integration Example
docs.text:
name: PR Checks

permissions:
  contents: read

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, develop ]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: '24'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint
      - name: Test
        run: npm test
      - name: Check coverage
        run: npm run coverage
      - name: Static analysis
        run: npm run analyze

This Node.js example assumes the repository defines the referenced scripts and lockfile. For workflows with elevated permissions or access to sensitive data, review GitHub guidance for untrusted pull-request code and token permissions before adapting it.

docs.title: Required Status Checks
docs.text:
Configure branch protection or rulesets to require: - All relevant CI checks pass - The required number of approvals for the change risk - Resolved review conversations where the team uses this control - A deliberate policy for dismissing stale approvals after material changes

Stale-review dismissal is a policy choice. Decide which changes should invalidate an approval and configure that behavior in the repository's protection rules.

docs.title: End-to-end review lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Prepare the change. Keep the pull request focused. Describe the problem, intended result, risk, test evidence, and rollout or migration plan. Split unrelated changes where practical.
  2. Choose reviewers. Request reviewers with the relevant context. Use CODEOWNERS for routing and repository rules for required approvals. Assign a driver to coordinate high-risk or cross-team changes.
  3. Review for substance. Check correctness, edge cases, tests, security and privacy, compatibility, operability, and whether the change solves the stated problem. Automate formatting and other mechanical checks.
  4. Make feedback actionable. State the concern and its impact, then suggest a change or ask a specific question. Label blocking concerns consistently. Use a synchronous discussion when written comments stop making progress.
  5. Resolve decisions. The author responds to comments and marks threads resolved when the concern is addressed or the reviewer agrees it is not blocking. Record material design decisions where future maintainers can find them.
  6. Confirm merge readiness. Verify required checks and approvals, review any changes since approval according to policy, and ensure rollout or database-migration steps are understood.
  7. Verify after merge. Monitor deployment and service signals for risky changes. Close the loop on incidents or follow-up work rather than assuming a green CI run proves production health.

For urgent fixes, define an explicit expedited path with an after-the-fact review and incident record. Do not silently bypass controls or treat a high-priority label as an approval.

docs.title: Constructive Feedback Framework
docs.text:
Elite teams follow a structured approach to feedback:

  1. Observation: Describe what you see in the code
  2. Impact: Explain the potential impact or concern
  3. Question or suggestion: Offer a constructive alternative
  4. Rationale: Provide reasoning or link to documentation

Example:

I notice this function mutates the input parameter (observation). This could lead to unexpected side effects for callers (impact). Could we create a copy of the object first before modifying it (suggestion)? This would maintain the principle of least surprise and prevent potential bugs (rationale).

docs.title: Feedback Anti-Patterns to Avoid
docs.text:
• Nitpicking: A comment such as “Use camelCase here” is better handled by a formatter or linter. Keep review attention on substantive behavior and design.
  • Vague feedback: Replace “This does not look right” with the concrete concern, such as “This approach might race when two requests update the record at the same time.”
  • Personal criticism: Focus on the code and its impact. Ask, “Could this approach make the behavior harder to test? Have you considered…?”
  • Overwhelming feedback: Prioritize blocking concerns and group related suggestions. For complex changes, pair or discuss the design rather than leaving dozens of disconnected comments.

docs.title: Pair Programming and Review
docs.text: For complex changes, elite teams use pair programming as a proactive review strategy: - Driver/Navigator: One person codes while the other reviews in real-time - Ping-Pong: Alternating between writing tests and implementation - Mob Programming: Multiple team members collaborate on a single change

docs.title: Review Workshops
docs.text: For architectural or high-impact changes: - Schedule dedicated review sessions - Use screen sharing and collaborative tools - Document decisions and rationales - Include stakeholders beyond the immediate team

docs.title: AI-Assisted Code Review
docs.text: Elite teams leverage AI tools to enhance (not replace) human review: - GitHub Copilot for code suggestions - Static analysis tools for common issues - Automated PR summaries for context - Vulnerability scanning for security issues

docs.title: Custom Review Automation
docs.text: Consider building custom tooling for project-specific needs: - Automated test generation - Documentation verification - API contract validation - Performance regression detection

docs.title: Small Team Approach (3-7 engineers)
docs.text: For small teams, focus on: - Everyone reviews everything (shared context) - Informal, frequent reviews - Synchronous pair reviews for complex changes - Simple tooling and minimal process

docs.title: Mid-Sized Team Approach (10-30 engineers)
docs.text: As teams grow: - Implement CODEOWNERS for domain expertise - Establish formal review protocols - Create specialized review checklists - Invest in automation and tooling

docs.title: Large Team Approach (30+ engineers)
docs.text: For large organizations: - Hierarchical review structure (team, domain, architecture) - Dedicated review teams for critical components - Comprehensive automation and metrics - Cross-team review coordination

docs.title: Process Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
• Rubber-stamping: Approvals without meaningful review
  • Review bottlenecks: PRs waiting days for review
  • Scope creep: Massive PRs that are impossible to review effectively
  • Ping-pong reviews: Endless back-and-forth without resolution
  • Tribal knowledge: Reviews that enforce undocumented standards

docs.title: Warning Signs in Review Culture
docs.text:
• Defensive responses to feedback
  • Reviews that focus only on style, not substance
  • Inconsistent standards between reviewers
  • Reviews becoming a blocker rather than an enabler
  • Lack of knowledge sharing during reviews

docs.title: Expert Notes: Code Review as a Learning Tool
docs.text:
Elite Team Insight: The most effective engineering teams view code review not just as quality control but as their primary knowledge-sharing mechanism. Reviews should be a conversation, not a gatekeeping exercise.

Scaling Tip: As your team grows beyond 10 engineers, invest early in automation and clear processes. The review patterns that work for a team of 5 will break down completely at 20+ engineers without deliberate scaling.

Cultural Note: Code review is where your engineering culture becomes visible. If reviews are respectful, thorough, and collaborative, that reflects a healthy engineering culture. If they're combative, superficial, or avoided, that signals deeper problems.

docs.title: Day 1 Setup
docs.text:
• Create basic PR template
  • Configure branch protection requiring reviews
  • Document review expectations in CONTRIBUTING.md
  • Set up essential CI checks (linting, tests)

docs.title: Small Team Evolution
docs.text:
• Implement review SLAs
  • Create specialized PR templates
  • Add code coverage checks
  • Establish review rotation

docs.title: Scaling to Mid-sized Teams
docs.text:
• Implement CODEOWNERS
  • Create domain-specific review checklists
  • Add advanced CI checks
  • Establish metrics for review quality and speed

docs.title: Large Organization Governance
docs.text:
• Create hierarchical review structure
  • Implement cross-team review coordination
  • Establish review standards and training
  • Build custom review automation

docs.title: GitHub Actions and Automation
docs.text: GitHub Actions can automate checks, releases, and deployments. A useful workflow gives fast, trustworthy feedback while keeping permissions and secrets limited to the jobs that need them. Examples below use current major action versions; review upstream release notes and pin actions to full commit SHAs when your supply-chain policy requires immutable references.

docs.title: A practical CI workflow
docs.text:
This example assumes a Node.js project with a committed package-lock.json and the lint, test, and build scripts in package.json. Change the scripts and supported Node.js versions to match the project.

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

Each job runs on a fresh runner. If checks are split into separate jobs, each job must check out the source and install its own dependencies. Jobs do not share a filesystem unless artifacts or another explicit storage mechanism is used. Add a concurrency group when newer commits should cancel superseded pull-request runs.

setup-node can cache package-manager data without a separate cache step. It does not cache node_modules. For repositories with elevated workflow permissions or sensitive data, disable automatic package-manager caching when it is not needed, and review cache access across branches and pull requests.1

For a Python project, use an explicit cache key and the correctly hyphenated restore-keys input:

- name: Cache Python downloads
  uses: actions/cache@v6
  with:
    path: ~/.cache/pip
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('**/requirements*.txt') }}
    restore-keys: |
      ${{ runner.os }}-pip-

A cache is an optimization, not a source of truth. Always install from a lockfile or pinned requirements and ensure a cache miss still produces a correct build.2

docs.title: Build and publish artifacts
docs.text:
Artifacts let one job pass build output to another job without rebuilding. Give each artifact a useful name and a deliberate retention period. Do not put credentials or other secrets in an artifact.

- name: Upload build output
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
  with:
    name: web-dist
    path: dist/
    if-no-files-found: error
    retention-days: 7

Use artifacts to transfer immutable build output between jobs, then deploy the exact artifact that passed the required checks. Do not assume a new runner contains output from a previous job.

docs.title: Deployment environments and approvals
docs.text:
Define environments such as staging and production in repository settings. Configure allowed branches, required reviewers, wait timers, and environment secrets there. The workflow's environment key selects an environment; it does not by itself create an approval rule. A job cannot access environment secrets until configured protection rules pass.3

Required reviewer availability and other environment features vary by repository visibility and plan. Check current GitHub plan limits before making an approval rule part of a release guarantee.3

docs.title: AWS deployment with OIDC
docs.text:
Prefer short-lived credentials through OpenID Connect (OIDC) over long-lived access keys. This example assumes the AWS identity provider, IAM role, trust policy, bucket, and GitHub environment have already been configured. The IAM trust policy should constrain access to the intended repository and branch or environment. Match the policy to the claims your GitHub organization actually emits; do not copy a generic subject claim without checking it.4

# .github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml
name: Deploy staging

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_STAGING_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION }}
      - name: Deploy
        env:
          BUCKET: ${{ vars.AWS_STAGING_BUCKET }}
        run: aws s3 sync dist/ "s3://${BUCKET}" --delete

The AWS credentials action requires aws-region. The role ARN is a configuration value rather than a password, so it can be stored as an environment variable. Keep the IAM role limited to the resources and operations the deployment needs. For production, use a separate role and environment, and configure production protection in repository settings.3

When an OIDC trust policy uses an environment, its subject claim identifies that environment. Branch restrictions may therefore need to be enforced on the GitHub environment as well as in AWS. Review current GitHub OIDC claim formats and AWS trust conditions when creating or changing the policy.4

docs.title: Rollback and release safety
docs.text:
Prefer versioned, immutable deployment artifacts. Deploy a known build, verify health after rollout, and keep a tested way to restore the previous version. Database changes need a compatibility and recovery plan; reverting application code alone may not reverse a schema change.

For higher-risk releases, use a staged rollout, health checks, and an explicit decision point before increasing traffic. Record who owns the rollback decision and how operators will trigger it. Avoid automatic rollback rules that can repeatedly flip a service without a human-visible incident signal.

docs.title: Code scanning with CodeQL
docs.text:
This example is for a JavaScript or TypeScript repository. Use CodeQL's supported language identifier and change the triggers and permissions to fit the repository.

# .github/workflows/codeql.yml
name: CodeQL

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '23 4 * * 1'

permissions:
  actions: read
  contents: read
  security-events: write

jobs:
  analyze:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v4
        with:
          languages: javascript-typescript
      - uses: github/codeql-action/autobuild@v4
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v4

Check the CodeQL documentation and action release notes for supported language identifiers, build requirements, and permissions before copying this workflow to another language or repository.5

docs.title: Reusable workflows
docs.text:
Put a reusable workflow in .github/workflows/ and declare its inputs and secrets under workflow_call. Keep permissions narrow in both the caller and reusable workflow. A called workflow cannot elevate the permissions granted by its caller.

# .github/workflows/reusable-node-checks.yml
name: Reusable Node checks

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version:
        required: false
        type: string
        default: '24'

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

Call it from another workflow with a job-level uses entry:

jobs:
  test:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-node-checks.yml
    with:
      node-version: '24'

Use reusable workflows for shared job-level procedures. Use a composite action when the reusable unit is a sequence of steps inside a job. Keep inputs explicit and version shared workflows when they are consumed across repositories.

docs.title: Set minimum permissions
docs.text: Start with read-only repository contents at workflow level. Grant additional scopes only to the job that needs them. OIDC deployment needs id-token: write; code scanning may need security-events: write. Avoid granting contents: write or broad organization permissions to routine test jobs.1

docs.title: Handle untrusted pull-request code safely
docs.text:
Treat pull-request titles, branch names, issue text, and source code as untrusted input. Do not interpolate attacker-controlled expressions directly into shell scripts. Pass values through environment variables and quote them, or use a safe action interface.

Workflows triggered by pull_request_target run with elevated access to the base repository. Do not check out and execute untrusted pull-request code in that privileged context. Prefer pull_request for ordinary validation, and review GitHub's secure-use guidance before using pull_request_target or workflow_run.1

docs.title: Protect secrets and credentials
docs.text:
• Store credentials in GitHub secrets or a supported identity federation flow. Never commit them or print them to logs.
  • Give each credential only the resource access required for its task. Rotate credentials if they are exposed.
  • Prefer environment-scoped deployment credentials and gate access to them with environment protection rules.
  • Do not run untrusted code in a job that can read deployment secrets.
  • Review third-party action source and permissions before adoption.

docs.title: Pin action dependencies
docs.text:
For a stricter supply-chain policy, pin each action to a full commit SHA from the action's own repository. A version comment helps maintainers update the pin deliberately. This checkout SHA is from the verified upstream v7.0.1 release:6

- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

A major-version tag such as @v7 is easier to update but can move as new releases are published. If using tags, review updates promptly and apply an automated dependency update process. GitHub's security guidance recommends full-length SHA pins where immutable action references are required.1

docs.title: Self-hosted runners
docs.text: Self-hosted runners can provide specialized hardware or access to private networks. They also retain more state and are not automatically isolated between jobs in the same way as fresh hosted runners. Do not use a persistent runner for untrusted pull-request code if it can access secrets, deployment credentials, or sensitive network resources. Keep runner images patched, restrict runner groups, and remove sensitive state after each job.1

docs.title: Troubleshooting and operations
docs.text:
Use the Actions run view to inspect logs and job summaries. The GitHub CLI can list and inspect runs:

gh run list
gh run view <run-id>

Track duration, failure rate, queue time, and flaky checks at workflow level. Fix recurring failures rather than normalizing retries. Keep logs useful, but do not print secrets or unnecessary personal data.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Start with read-only token permissions and expand per job only as required.
  • Check out code and install dependencies independently in every job that needs them.
  • Commit lockfiles and verify that cache misses do not change build correctness.
  • Transfer build output explicitly with artifacts when jobs are separated.
  • Configure environment approvals and branch restrictions in repository settings.
  • Prefer OIDC or short-lived credentials over stored cloud access keys.
  • Keep untrusted pull-request code away from privileged workflows and persistent runners.
  • Pin actions to verified full commit SHAs when policy requires immutable dependencies.
  • Test deployment, health checks, and rollback procedures before relying on them.

docs.title: Governance and Security
docs.text: Repository governance should make safe work the normal path without adding controls that do not reduce a clear risk. Set a small organizational baseline, document exceptions, and review the controls when ownership or system risk changes.

docs.title: Repository baseline
docs.text:
A service or library may use a structure like this, adapted to its build system:

.github/
  ISSUE_TEMPLATE/
  workflows/
  PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
  CODEOWNERS
docs/
src/
tests/
scripts/
CHANGELOG.md
CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
CONTRIBUTING.md
LICENSE
README.md
SECURITY.md

Use repository templates or an internal starter repository to make the baseline easy to adopt. Keep templates maintained, and avoid requiring files that do not fit the project.

docs.title: Branch protection and repository rules
docs.text:
Protect important branches such as main with pull-request review and required checks. Choose the number and type of approvals based on change risk and team size. Require checks that actually run for that branch, and periodically remove obsolete check names so the merge queue cannot become stuck.

Consider requiring resolved conversations, linear history, signed commits, or restricted push access when they solve a defined need. Document who can bypass a rule and how emergency changes are reviewed afterward. Rulesets and branch protection offer overlapping controls; verify the exact feature availability and scope in repository settings before standardizing a policy across an organization.

docs.title: Signed commits
docs.text: A signed-commit requirement checks that commits have a signature GitHub can verify. A verified signature is useful evidence about the signing key and integrity of the commit. It does not by itself prove that the named author personally created the change or that the change was reviewed. Treat commit signing as one control, not a replacement for review, access control, or audit.

docs.title: CODEOWNERS
docs.text:
A CODEOWNERS file routes review requests for paths. Put it in .github/CODEOWNERS, the repository root, or docs/CODEOWNERS; GitHub uses the first one it finds in that order. Owners must have write access, and teams must be visible and have explicit write access to the repository.1

# .github/CODEOWNERS
# Default owner for files not matched below
* @example-org/maintainers

# More specific rules override the earlier matching rule
/docs/ @example-org/docs-team
/src/frontend/ @example-org/frontend-team
/src/backend/ @example-org/backend-team @example-org/security-team
/.github/CODEOWNERS @example-org/maintainers

The last matching pattern takes precedence. Patterns follow most, but not all, .gitignore behavior. In particular, do not use ^ to make an owner optional or ! to negate a pattern. CODEOWNERS paths are case-sensitive. If multiple owners appear on one matching line, any one of them can satisfy a required code-owner approval; the rule does not require every listed owner to approve.1

A CODEOWNERS entry alone does not prevent merging. Enable required code-owner review in branch protection or an applicable ruleset when owner approval must be a merge requirement. Keep the CODEOWNERS file itself owned so a change cannot silently remove review routing.1

docs.title: Access management
docs.text:
Grant each person and team the least repository role needed for their work. Prefer team-based access over repeated individual grants in an organization. Remove access when responsibilities end, and review outside collaborators, deploy keys, GitHub Apps, machine users, and personal access tokens on a regular schedule.

Use a consistent process for requesting and approving access. Separate routine contribution from administration: only a small set of trusted maintainers should manage repository settings, rulesets, secrets, and runner groups. Document break-glass access and review its use afterward.

Before rolling out a role model, check the exact permissions attached to the role in the current GitHub settings. Role names and available controls can differ between organization and personal repositories and between GitHub plans.

docs.title: Security reporting and maintenance
docs.text:
Add a SECURITY.md file that explains supported versions, the private vulnerability-reporting path, and the expected response process. Use private vulnerability reporting or a GitHub Security Advisory where available. Do not ask reporters to publish exploit details in a public issue.

Enable Dependabot alerts to identify vulnerable dependencies. Security updates can open pull requests for vulnerable dependencies when enabled, while version updates keep dependencies current through dependabot.yml. Confirm the dependency graph, alerts, security-update setting, and version-update configuration separately. Review proposed updates before merging them.2

# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: weekly

Adapt package ecosystems and directories to the repository. Use pull-request review, CI, and a plan for handling breaking updates instead of auto-merging every dependency change without qualification.

docs.title: Secrets and Actions policy
docs.text:
Store secrets at the narrowest practical scope. Prefer environment-scoped secrets for deployments and short-lived credentials through OIDC for cloud access. Limit GITHUB_TOKEN permissions in workflow files and avoid running untrusted pull-request code in privileged contexts. Review third-party actions before use and require verified full-length commit SHA pins if the organization's supply-chain policy calls for immutable action references.3

For self-hosted runners, restrict which repositories and workflows can use each runner group. Keep runners patched, prevent untrusted code from reaching persistent state, and remove credentials and workspace data after a job.

docs.title: Auditing and exceptions
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory of repositories, owners, criticality, and the controls that apply. Review membership and access grants periodically. Use organization audit logs where available to investigate settings changes, access changes, and sensitive administrative actions.

Record exceptions with an owner, reason, compensating control, and review date. Remove exceptions when the underlying need ends. When a control blocks routine work, confirm whether the rule is misconfigured or too broad before weakening a security requirement.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Protect production branches with appropriate pull-request reviews and required checks.
  • Give teams and users only the access they need, and review grants regularly.
  • Use CODEOWNERS for routing and repository rules for required approvals.
  • Protect the CODEOWNERS file and workflow definitions from unreviewed changes.
  • Publish a private security reporting path and define supported versions.
  • Enable and configure Dependabot alerts and version updates separately.
  • Limit workflow token permissions and use scoped, short-lived deployment credentials.
  • Document rule bypasses, exceptions, and emergency review procedures.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Repository boundaries shape code ownership, access control, build and release workflows, and the cost of cross-team changes. There is no universally best monorepo or polyrepo model. Choose the simplest structure that fits product boundaries, team responsibilities, security needs, and release cadence, then revisit the decision as those conditions change.

This guide covers the choice between monorepos and polyrepos, repository layout, dependency practices, visibility, and discovery. It is a decision and implementation guide, not a prescription based on headcount alone.

docs.title: Monorepo
docs.text:
A monorepo stores multiple related applications, libraries, or services in one Git repository. It can make atomic cross-project changes and shared tooling easier. It also increases the need for clear ownership, selective builds, and access-control design.

A monorepo is a good candidate when projects frequently change together, share internal packages, or benefit from common build and test tooling. It is a poor fit when projects require sharply different access boundaries, have unrelated release and ownership models, or cannot be isolated by the available tooling.

docs.title: Polyrepo
docs.text:
A polyrepo model gives each service, product, or library its own repository. This supports independent permissions, ownership, and releases. It adds work for cross-repository changes, shared tooling, dependency upgrades, and organization-wide discovery.

Polyrepo can work well when components have independent lifecycles, different security requirements, or distinct maintainer communities. It is not automatically faster: build time depends on the project and CI design, not only on repository count.

docs.title: Hybrid model
docs.text: A hybrid model uses a monorepo for tightly coupled applications and shared libraries while keeping independently governed products or infrastructure in separate repositories. Define the boundary explicitly. Avoid splitting a codebase solely because one team or one tool prefers it.

docs.title: Decision questions
docs.text:
Before choosing or changing a boundary, answer:

  1. Which components routinely need to change and deploy together?
  2. Who owns each component, and can ownership be represented clearly in the chosen structure?
  3. Do teams need separate read/write access or different compliance controls?
  4. Can the build system identify affected projects and reuse build outputs safely?
  5. How will dependencies be versioned, upgraded, and supported?
  6. How will engineers discover a repository, its owners, deployment path, dependencies, and support channel?
  7. What migration cost and operational burden will the new boundary create?

Record the decision, assumptions, and signals that would trigger a review. Re-evaluate using actual change and operational data rather than a generic team-size threshold.

docs.title: Application repository
docs.text:
service-name/
├── .github/
│   ├── ISSUE_TEMPLATE/
│   ├── workflows/
│   └── PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
├── docs/
├── src/
├── tests/
├── scripts/
├── config/
├── .gitignore
├── CONTRIBUTING.md
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
├── SECURITY.md
└── package.json or pyproject.toml or go.mod

Treat dist/, build/, target/, coverage output, and other generated files as build outputs. Commit them only when the publishing or runtime model specifically requires it; otherwise ignore them and publish versioned artifacts from CI.

docs.title: Monorepo
docs.text:
product/
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/
│   └── admin/
├── services/
│   ├── billing/
│   └── identity/
├── packages/
│   └── shared-ui/
├── infra/
├── tools/
├── docs/
├── CODEOWNERS
├── package.json
└── workspace-config.json

Group code by deployable or owned unit. Give each unit a clear owner and an explicit dependency direction. Keep shared libraries small and intentional. Use a workspace/build tool that supports affected-project detection, caching, and dependency graphs when repository size makes full builds too expensive.

docs.title: Library repository
docs.text:
library-name/
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
├── docs/
├── examples/
├── src/
├── tests/
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── CONTRIBUTING.md
├── LICENSE
├── README.md
└── package.json or pyproject.toml or go.mod

Document the supported runtime and compatibility policy. Test published packages from the built artifact, not only from the source checkout.

docs.title: Monorepo implementation
docs.text:
Use a workspace or build system that matches the ecosystem and scale. Nx, Turborepo, Bazel, Gradle, and language-native workspaces solve overlapping but not identical problems. Compare setup cost, incremental correctness, remote-cache trust, supported languages, local developer workflow, and maintenance ownership before adopting one.

A practical rollout is:

  1. Map packages, deployable units, dependencies, and owners.
  2. Establish a consistent package and test layout before moving code.
  3. Introduce workspace tooling and make local commands work without CI-specific assumptions.
  4. Add CI that tests affected projects and a scheduled or protected full-suite run.
  5. Cache only reproducible inputs and outputs; include toolchain and lockfile state in cache keys.
  6. Publish artifacts with immutable versions and explicit provenance.
  7. Track cross-project build time, cache hit rate, flaky tests, and ownership gaps.

Do not use path filters as the only correctness guard if changes can affect shared tooling or downstream projects. Include shared configuration in the affected-project graph or run broader checks when impact cannot be determined.

docs.title: Polyrepo implementation
docs.text:
Standardize the minimum needed to make repositories predictable while allowing teams to choose their own implementation details. A shared template can provide repository metadata, contribution and security files, baseline CI, branch rules, and dependency automation.

For shared packages, publish immutable versions to an appropriate registry and use each consumer's lockfile or dependency lock mechanism. Define compatibility and deprecation policies. Avoid cross-repository coordination based on unversioned branches or undocumented manual steps.

Where coordinated releases are required, use an explicit release plan, compatible version ranges, and an integration environment. For automation between repositories, scope credentials narrowly, make operations idempotent, and define what happens when one step fails.

docs.title: Dependency and supply-chain practices
docs.text:
• Commit the ecosystem's lockfile where applicable and keep it in sync with dependency manifests.
  • Use supported version ranges or exact versions according to the package manager and release policy; do not apply a single pinning rule to every ecosystem.
  • Automate update proposals, then test and review them. Separate urgent security fixes from routine upgrades.
  • Scan the relevant artifact types: source-code analysis, dependency vulnerabilities, container images, and infrastructure configuration are different checks.
  • Generate an SBOM when a product, customer, or regulatory requirement justifies it. State the format, scope, and release to which it applies.
  • Protect build credentials, registries, caches, and release artifacts. Define who can publish and how compromised credentials are revoked.

docs.title: Visibility and discoverability
docs.text:
Choose public, internal, or private visibility according to data classification, open-source intent, customer commitments, and access needs. Visibility does not replace permissions for sensitive actions or secrets. Review visibility when ownership or product scope changes.

Every repository should make these items easy to find:

  • Purpose, lifecycle status, and supported versions.
  • Owning team and a support or escalation path.
  • Setup, test, build, and release commands.
  • Deployment target and operational dashboard or runbook.
  • Dependencies, APIs, and consumers where material.
  • Contribution and security-reporting instructions.

For larger estates, maintain a service catalog or repository index with ownership, criticality, dependencies, deployment status, and documentation links. Assign an owner to keep that metadata current. Innersource works when contribution expectations, review ownership, and support commitments are clear; visibility alone does not create collaboration.

docs.title: Common failure patterns
docs.text:
• Repositories grouped by current team structure even though ownership boundaries change frequently.
  • A monorepo without affected-project checks, module ownership, or a reliable local workflow.
  • Polyrepos that duplicate workflow policy while allowing security controls to drift.
  • Shared libraries published without compatibility guarantees or a maintainer.
  • Generated build outputs committed accidentally or used as the only release artifact.
  • A service catalog with no owner or update process.
  • Repository migrations performed without a rollback plan, redirect strategy, or dependency inventory.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Write down the boundary decision and the conditions that would change it.
  • Identify owners for each repository, service, package, and sensitive path.
  • Standardize the minimum repository metadata and onboarding commands.
  • Ensure dependencies and build outputs are reproducible and distinguishable.
  • Add CI checks appropriate to the repository's risk and release model.
  • Document release, rollback, and support paths.
  • Add repositories and services to a maintained discovery index.
  • Review the structure after significant changes to teams, products, access needs, or deployment cadence.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-24

docs.title: Metrics & Developer Experience: Measuring What Matters
Purpose and guardrails
docs.text:
Engineering metrics are useful when they help a team find friction, test an improvement, and learn whether it worked. They become harmful when treated as a ranking of individuals, a quota, or a substitute for understanding the system. Use quantitative measures together with team conversations and product context.

Define each measure before collecting it: population, event boundaries, time window, data source, exclusions, and owner. Keep definitions stable enough to compare trends, and disclose changes to the calculation.

docs.title: DORA software delivery performance
docs.text:
DORA's current software delivery framework describes five metrics. The definitions below follow its current guide; apply them to a product or service and interpret trends in context.1

  1. Change lead time measures the time from a change being committed to version control until it is deployed to production. Define what event identifies the change and how batched changes are attributed to a deployment.
  2. Deployment frequency measures production deployments over a period or the time between deployments. Decide which production changes count, including configuration or data changes.
  3. Failed deployment recovery time measures time to recover from a deployment failure that requires immediate intervention. Define what qualifies as intervention and what event marks recovery.
  4. Change fail rate measures the share of deployments that require immediate intervention, such as a rollback or hotfix. Define how failures are attributed when the cause is uncertain.
  5. Deployment rework rate measures the share of unplanned deployments made because of a production incident. Distinguish incident-driven rework from planned follow-up work.

Do not mix failed-deployment recovery time with general incident MTTR without defining the difference. Agree on data boundaries with the people who operate the service. Start with a small number of services and validate the calculations manually before building dashboards.

DORA cautions against using the metrics as universal targets or comparing unlike applications. A service-level trend and a discussion about what changed are more useful than a league table. Avoid targets that reward deployment count or penalize teams for the risk profile they have inherited.1

docs.title: A practical measurement cycle
docs.text:
1. Choose one service and name the team accountable for improving its delivery system.
  2. Write a metric dictionary with formulas, event sources, scope, exclusions, and known data gaps.
  3. Establish a baseline over a representative period. Mark incidents, migrations, and instrumentation changes that affect interpretation.
  4. Discuss bottlenecks with the team. Use measures to locate questions, not to assign blame.
  5. Select one change to the system, such as smaller batch sizes, faster tests, or clearer deployment ownership.
  6. Review the result after a suitable interval. Keep, adapt, or revert the intervention based on both outcomes and team experience.
  7. Repeat, updating definitions only through a documented change.

docs.title: Developer experience
docs.text:
Developer experience (DevEx) is shaped by the daily ability to make progress: cognitive load, feedback speed, tool reliability, documentation, onboarding, and collaboration. No single proxy captures it. Pair surveys and interviews with operational signals such as setup time, CI duration, flaky-test rate, time spent waiting for reviews, and repeated support requests.

The SPACE framework is one way to organize measurement across Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, and Efficiency. Use it as a prompt to consider several dimensions, not as a requirement to score every developer or collect every available event. Activity counts, including commits and pull requests, are particularly easy to misinterpret without outcome and workload context.

docs.title: Example survey
docs.text:
Use consistent wording and a short response scale, and allow respondents to skip questions. Explain who can see raw responses, how they will be reported, and what action may follow. Do not promise anonymity if the sample size or collection method cannot provide it.

Ask respondents to rate each statement from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with an optional “not applicable” response:

  1. I can make a small change and get useful feedback quickly.
  2. Our local development environment is reliable and documented.
  3. CI results are trustworthy and failures are actionable.
  4. I can find the owner and support path for the systems I work on.
  5. The tools I use fit together without unnecessary context switching.
  6. Reviews help me improve the change without avoidable delay.
  7. I have enough uninterrupted time to complete important work.
  8. I can raise a reliability or security concern without blame.
  9. On-call and operational responsibilities are manageable.
  10. What is the most frequent source of avoidable waiting?
  11. What tool or process most often interrupts your work?
  12. What one change would most improve your ability to deliver safely?

Review themes at team level. Share the response rate, the main themes, and the actions the team has chosen. Follow up to learn whether the change helped. Suppress or combine small groups when reporting could identify a respondent.

docs.title: Balanced team scorecard
docs.text:
A useful review combines a small set of outcome and experience signals. For example, a team may consider delivery flow, service reliability, customer outcomes, review health, onboarding friction, and team sustainability. The exact measures should reflect the service and the questions the team is trying to answer.

Avoid making individual performance decisions from raw GitHub activity, lines of code, commit counts, or uncontextualized pull-request counts. If individual development conversations use work data, discuss it with the person, account for role and opportunity differences, and include qualitative evidence and outcomes.

docs.title: Instrumentation and data quality
docs.text:
Before automating a dashboard, answer:

  • Is the source event authoritative, and can the calculation be reproduced?
  • Are deployment events linked to the code changes and incidents they concern?
  • Are time zones, calendar windows, canceled releases, hotfixes, and rollbacks handled consistently?
  • Can contributors correct missing or misattributed data?
  • Are access, retention, and aggregation appropriate for workforce-related information?
  • What does the metric not tell us?

A lightweight dashboard can start from GitHub pull requests and deployment records, but neither API fields nor event timestamps are a complete definition by themselves. Add pagination, error handling, time-window boundaries, and service-specific attribution before relying on automated values. If data quality is weak, use a manual sample and improve instrumentation before presenting precise scores.

docs.title: Implementation checklist
docs.text:
• Choose a service-level improvement question rather than a generic ranking target.
  • Document metric definitions, boundaries, data sources, owners, and limitations.
  • Validate a sample of events manually before publishing a dashboard.
  • Pair delivery measures with reliability and developer-experience signals.
  • Review trends with the team and agree on a specific improvement.
  • Explain survey privacy, reporting, response-rate, and follow-up practices.
  • Do not use activity counts or DORA bands as individual quotas.
  • Revisit definitions and data quality when the product, release model, or instrumentation changes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Organization structure, access rules, and project tracking should make ownership and delivery visible without creating needless hierarchy. This guide provides a practical starting point for GitHub organizations, teams, permissions, Projects, and cross-repository planning. Adapt the examples to the organization’s identity, compliance, and release requirements.

docs.title: Organization and team structure
docs.text:
Use an organization boundary for a meaningful security, ownership, or administration boundary. Within an organization, create teams around durable ownership domains such as a product area, platform capability, or service group. Avoid a deep team hierarchy that merely mirrors reporting lines.

A team should have a named maintainer, a clear purpose, and a documented set of repositories or responsibilities. Use parent/child teams only when they improve discovery or permission management. For cross-functional work, add collaborators to a project or issue rather than creating a permanent team with no continuing ownership.

Before choosing one or several organizations, consider:

  • Whether repositories need separate visibility, policies, billing, or administrators.
  • Whether teams can share repositories and enterprise policy while retaining clear ownership.
  • How identity-provider synchronization, offboarding, and audit requirements will work.
  • Whether cross-organization collaboration will create duplicate permissions or workflow complexity.

docs.title: Access-control model
docs.text:
Grant the least access needed for a person or team to perform its work. Prefer team-based repository permissions over individually managed access. Review access when people change roles and on a regular schedule. Use a time-bounded process for exceptional elevated access and record who approved it and why.

  • Organization owner: reserve for a small number of trusted administrators. Confirm that each owner needs organization-wide configuration access.
  • Repository administrator: use for repository settings and access management. Delegate narrower responsibilities when practical.
  • Maintainer or write access: use for normal contribution and review. Confirm that the team needs write access to each repository in the grant.
  • Triage access: use for issue and pull-request management when direct code changes are not required.
  • Read access: use for consumers, auditors, or contributors who do not need to write. Check that repository visibility fits the intended audience.

The names and capabilities of roles can differ by plan and product settings. Validate permissions in the organization before applying a template. Keep emergency access separate from normal day-to-day access and review its use afterward.

docs.title: Repository ownership and CODEOWNERS
docs.text:
Keep repository owners, CODEOWNERS entries, and team memberships aligned. A CODEOWNERS file requests reviews from owners; it does not itself block a merge. If owner approval is required, enable the corresponding required-code-owner-review rule in branch protection or a repository ruleset. Owners and teams need appropriate repository access, and the CODEOWNERS file must be present on the pull request’s base branch.

Use valid GitHub usernames or organization-qualified team names. For example:

# .github/CODEOWNERS
*                       @example-org/repo-maintainers
/docs/                  @example-org/documentation
/services/billing/      @example-org/billing-team
/.github/workflows/     @example-org/platform-security

Review the file when teams, paths, or ownership change. Use branch rules to protect sensitive ownership and workflow files themselves.

docs.title: GitHub Projects as a planning layer
docs.text:
Use a Project when a team needs a shared view across issues, pull requests, repositories, or iterations. Start with the minimum fields needed to answer the team’s planning questions. For example:

  • Status: Backlog, Ready, In progress, In review, Done.
  • Priority: A small, agreed scale that identifies sequencing rather than individual performance.
  • Iteration: A timebox only when the team actually plans work in iterations.
  • Owner: The person or team coordinating the next action.
  • Target date or milestone: A commitment with a clear decision-maker and review cadence.

A Kanban team can use a board with explicit work-in-progress limits. A team using Scrum can connect iteration planning to a defined goal, backlog, and review. A roadmap can show outcomes, dependencies, and confidence ranges without treating estimated dates as guarantees. Choose one process model that fits the team; avoid keeping duplicate status fields in both the project and the issue tracker unless ownership is explicit.

docs.title: Issue and pull-request templates
docs.text:
A good issue template captures the information needed to route and assess work without forcing every request into a long form. A feature request might ask for the problem, intended outcome, constraints, and acceptance criteria. A bug report should request reproduction steps, expected and observed behavior, affected version, and relevant logs with sensitive values removed.

Pull-request templates should prompt authors to explain the change, link related work, describe tests, identify risk, and note rollout or migration requirements where relevant. Do not make checkboxes a substitute for review; remove questions that do not influence a decision.

docs.title: Cross-repository initiatives
docs.text:
For work spanning multiple repositories, designate one parent issue or project item as the coordination record. Link implementation issues in each repository and state the dependency order, owner, integration criteria, and release sequence. Keep local work actionable in its own repository. Update the parent when scope, owner, or dependency dates change.

Use epics, milestones, and roadmaps to answer different questions:

  • An epic groups related implementation work toward an outcome.
  • A milestone or iteration groups work for a release or timebox.
  • A roadmap communicates intended outcomes, sequencing, dependencies, and confidence.

Avoid copying the same long description into many issues. Link to the source of truth and keep a concise summary in each work item.

docs.title: Operating cadence and reporting
docs.text: Set a planning cadence suited to the work. At each review, confirm ownership, priority, dependencies, and whether the work still supports the intended outcome. Close or re-scope stale items. Use cycle time and work-in-progress data to identify flow problems, not to rank individuals. Keep project status useful to contributors by limiting manual updates and automating only reliable transitions.

docs.title: Adoption checklist
docs.text:
• Define organization boundaries, administrators, and team ownership.
  • Apply repository access through durable teams where practical.
  • Document how access is requested, approved, reviewed, and removed.
  • Use branch rules and CODEOWNERS together where owner approval is required.
  • Choose a single source of truth for each planning field.
  • Make cross-repository dependencies and integration ownership explicit.
  • Review stale issues, permissions, teams, and project fields periodically.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-24

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: GitHub can be the source repository and automation hub while other services support planning, code quality, observability, or developer workflows. Add an integration only when it solves a defined problem that GitHub or the current toolchain does not already solve well. More integrations also mean more credentials, data copies, failure modes, and maintenance.

docs.title: Choose tools by capability
docs.text:
• Planning and issue tracking: GitHub Issues and Projects, Linear, or Jira. Decide which system owns status, priority, and identifiers, and how cross-repository work is linked.
  • Documentation and knowledge: repository Markdown, a documentation platform, or a knowledge base. Decide which content must be versioned with code and who maintains external links and access.
  • Code quality and coverage: CodeQL, Codecov, SonarQube, SonarCloud, or Codacy. Confirm language coverage, the required quality gate, and ownership of false positives.
  • Error reporting and product signals: Sentry, LogRocket, or platform-native observability. Review collected data, access, retention, privacy, and incident ownership.
  • Source search and discovery: GitHub search, Sourcegraph, or a service catalog. Check repository coverage, index freshness, and protection of private results.
  • Release and package distribution: GitHub Releases, a package registry, or an artifact repository. Define who can publish and how versions, provenance, retention, and rollback are managed.

These are examples, not endorsements. Product features, plans, and integration behavior change. Validate the specific capability, permissions, data handling, and support commitment before standardizing a tool.

docs.title: Preserve a clear source of truth
docs.text: Choose one system to own each important record. If an issue is mirrored between GitHub and another tracker, define which side is authoritative for description, status, and closure. Document synchronization direction, field mapping, conflict behavior, and expected delay. Avoid a two-way sync unless conflicts are explicitly handled.

docs.title: Scope credentials narrowly
docs.text: Use the integration’s narrowest supported permissions. Store credentials in the appropriate secret store, rotate them, and make ownership explicit. Prefer short-lived identity federation when supported over long-lived broad-scope tokens. Never expose credentials to untrusted pull-request code or publish them in logs.

docs.title: Make automation safe to retry
docs.text: Webhook delivery and CI jobs can be delayed, duplicated, or retried. Use stable event identifiers, idempotent updates, bounded retries, and visible failure handling. Do not silently discard a failed sync or deployment notification; route it to an owner and provide a recovery path.

docs.title: Keep sensitive data in scope
docs.text: Before connecting a tool, review what repository content, code, issue metadata, telemetry, or user data it can access. Determine where that data is stored, who can view it, and how it can be deleted. Apply retention and privacy requirements to logs, crash reports, and AI services as well as the Git repository.

docs.title: Avoid gates that no one owns
docs.text: A status check should have a named owner, a documented purpose, and an agreed failure response. Review flaky or redundant checks. Separate advisory signals from checks that block merging so teams understand which requirements are mandatory.

docs.title: Common integration patterns
docs.text:
• Issue tracker link: Include the external issue key in branch or pull-request metadata, then link records in both systems. Decide whether issue closure follows merge or release.
  • Coverage and analysis: Run checks on pull requests, publish a readable report, and make only defined thresholds blocking. Establish ownership for baseline updates and false positives.
  • Error tracking: Include release or commit identifiers in deployments so an incident can be connected to the code and rollout. Restrict access to customer data and redact secrets or personal information.
  • Repository mirroring: Treat a mirror as a backup or distribution channel with a documented one-way source of truth. Define credential rotation and the response to divergence.
  • CLI automation: Use the GitHub CLI for repeatable developer actions, but avoid embedding personal tokens in scripts. Provide tested commands, expected permissions, and an error path.

docs.title: Build an integration inventory
docs.text:
For each integration, record:

  1. Business or engineering purpose and accountable owner.
  2. Systems, repositories, and data it can access.
  3. Authentication method and permission scope.
  4. Source-of-truth and synchronization behavior.
  5. Availability, failure, retry, and manual recovery expectations.
  6. Cost, retention, privacy, and vendor exit considerations.
  7. Review date and decommissioning procedure.

Review this inventory when an integration changes scope, credentials, owner, or data classification. Remove unused applications and revoke their access.

docs.title: Selection checklist
docs.text:
• The need is specific and not already covered by an existing supported tool.
  • The integration has an owner and a maintained support path.
  • The data flow and permissions are understood and documented.
  • Automation is safe under duplicate events, retries, and partial failure.
  • Blocking checks have actionable failure messages and explicit ownership.
  • The team can export or recover important records if the service is unavailable.
  • Costs and security/privacy requirements have been reviewed.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-24
